03-infra-management.notes: Closest call: G vs E, both 8.75. G is slightly more correct (TCP pg_isready vs E's socket probe); E has the richer runbook. G wins on the higher-weighted criterion. L, H and C sit at 8.5. H has the deepest hardening and a verify script that passes 69/69, but loses on a static upstream (manual proxy restart after api recreate) and host-shell variable bugs in its runbook. L and C are cleaner but less hardened. A and J have arguably the best runbooks and hardening, but both use `redis-cli --host`. redis-cli only accepts -h: an unknown long option is rejected, or at best sent as a command, so PONG never appears. Their cache can therefore never become healthy, and the service_healthy chain blocks api and proxy. I could not run redis-cli here (no daemon, binary or network), so this rests on knowledge of redis-cli's option parsing. Even under the most lenient interpretation the output is not PONG. A's read-only, non-root nginx also very likely fails creating the default fastcgi/uwsgi/scgi temp dirs under /var/cache/nginx. This is also unverified without an nginx binary, but it is why J and H moved all five temp paths. B's Redis URL bug was confirmed by simulation (about 49% of base64 secrets contain '/', which breaks urlparse). Nothing could be built or run: no Docker daemon, nginx, redis-cli or Python web packages are available. All scoring rests on `docker compose config` renders (all 12 pass with dummy secrets), running the submissions' own tests and scripts (J 10/10, H 69/69), and static review. Most submissions (C, E, G, H, I, K, L) supply no application and assume a /healthz endpoint. That is reasonable since none was provided, and each one documents it. A, B, F and J added minimal app.py stand-ins.

12-frontend-editorial.notes: A vs E was the closest call at the top: E is the most typographically careful, but A has the stronger display motif, two reading controls and better validation, and E overflows at 320px. I, B and C tie at 8.25. I ranks first on its motif and two reading controls despite breaking at tablet width; B beats C because its reading mode changes more and it has no text under 12px. D and K tie at 7.5; D ranks higher for its artwork, while K is held back by an invented excerpt and pull-quote and a misleading 'checkout link on its way' message. Every submission passed the objective checks (no overflow at 390/1440, no remote requests, no console errors under file://). Over http, C and H logged a favicon 404, which was ignored. Not verified: real screen-reader output (judged from the DOM and ARIA only) and rendering with the intended system fonts (Iowan, Baskerville etc. fall back on this Linux machine). D and G share very similar structure and code; each was scored on its own merits. F's process note (writing outside its task directory) was docked under implementation quality.

Every required flow worked in my tests, along with extras that also work (adding observations, a U shortcut for undo), and I found no contrast or focus defects. It is the most complete and best-judged submission.

13-frontend-playful.notes: A against C was the closest call. Both are distinctive, complete and well composed on desktop. A wins on accessibility details (no undersized targets, focus moves to the next action) and on extras that work (adding observations, the U shortcut). C has the boldest look but a 60x23 name button. B and K tie at 9.0: B's desktop composition and polish put it ahead of K, though K is more accessible and closer to the 'odd' brief. Cross-cutting checks: every submission inlines its data, makes no network requests and has reduced-motion CSS (no animation over 50ms ran under reducedMotion: reduce). D, G and J drop focus to <body> after the main action. G and J use the wrong action verb for non-water tasks. H's snooze path cannot reach all-done. Some apps use the real clock (D, H, I, K, E), so dates differ from the provided screenshots; I did not penalise that heavily. Contrast was checked against the nearest solid ancestor background, ignoring gradients and images, so the figures are approximate. Screen-reader output was not checked with assistive technology, only through aria attributes and live-region text.
